```{r setup, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(caret)
library(Metrics)
library(randomForest)

set.seed(42)

# Load + drop the hamster
coffee_clean <- read_csv("df_coffee_cleaned.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  filter(Processing_clean != "Other")

# Fit M1 (full data)
m1 <- lm(`Total Cup Points` ~ Altitude_m + Variety_clean + Processing_clean +
                              Color_clean + `Moisture Percentage` +
                              `Category One Defects` + `Category Two Defects`,
         data = coffee_clean)

# Fit M2
m2 <- lmer(`Total Cup Points` ~ Altitude_m + Variety_clean + Processing_clean +
                                Color_clean + `Moisture Percentage` +
                                `Category One Defects` + `Category Two Defects` +
                                (1 | `Country of Origin`),
           data = coffee_clean)

varcomp <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m2))
icc <- varcomp$vcov[1] / sum(varcomp$vcov)

# Train/test
train_idx <- createDataPartition(coffee_clean$`Total Cup Points`, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train_data <- coffee_clean[train_idx, ]
test_data  <- coffee_clean[-train_idx, ]

m1_train <- lm(formula(m1), data = train_data)
m2_train <- lmer(formula(m2), data = train_data)
m1_preds <- predict(m1_train, newdata = test_data)
m2_preds <- predict(m2_train, newdata = test_data, allow.new.levels = TRUE)
m1_rmse <- rmse(test_data$`Total Cup Points`, m1_preds)
m2_rmse <- rmse(test_data$`Total Cup Points`, m2_preds)

# RF
train_rf <- train_data %>%
  select(`Total Cup Points`, Altitude_m, Variety_clean, Processing_clean,
         Color_clean, `Moisture Percentage`, `Category One Defects`,
         `Category Two Defects`, `Country of Origin`) %>%
  rename(TCP = `Total Cup Points`, Moisture = `Moisture Percentage`,
         Defects_1 = `Category One Defects`, Defects_2 = `Category Two Defects`,
         Country = `Country of Origin`) %>%
  mutate(across(c(Variety_clean, Processing_clean, Color_clean, Country), as.factor))

test_rf <- test_data %>%
  select(`Total Cup Points`, Altitude_m, Variety_clean, Processing_clean,
         Color_clean, `Moisture Percentage`, `Category One Defects`,
         `Category Two Defects`, `Country of Origin`) %>%
  rename(TCP = `Total Cup Points`, Moisture = `Moisture Percentage`,
         Defects_1 = `Category One Defects`, Defects_2 = `Category Two Defects`,
         Country = `Country of Origin`) %>%
  mutate(across(c(Variety_clean, Processing_clean, Color_clean, Country), as.factor))

for (col in c("Variety_clean", "Processing_clean", "Color_clean", "Country")) {
  levels(test_rf[[col]]) <- levels(train_rf[[col]])
}

set.seed(42)
rf_model <- randomForest(TCP ~ ., data = train_rf, ntree = 500, importance = TRUE)
rf_preds <- predict(rf_model, newdata = test_rf)
rf_rmse <- rmse(test_rf$TCP, rf_preds)
```

## 💡 Brewing the Real Question {.smaller}

> **Can sensory-independent variables — country, altitude, variety, processing, and physical bean characteristics — predict the Total Cup Points of specialty Arabica coffee?**

In other words: 🕵️ *Can we tell how a coffee will score WITHOUT ever tasting it?*

. . .

🔄 **the difference from my first question:**

❌ **before:** taste scores predicting total = tautology

✅ **now:** non-taste info predicting total = actual modeling

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
![](pour_coffee.jpeg){width="20%"}
:::

## 🎯 What I'm Bean-Hypothesizing {.smaller}

*Hypotheses = my educated guesses BEFORE running models. Each one gets tested by one of my 3 models 👇*

**H1** — Growing-region and processing variables (altitude, variety, processing) significantly predict Total Cup Points.

**H2** — Country of origin explains *additional* variance beyond those.

**H3** — A random forest model predicts better on held-out data than multiple linear regression.

. . .

:::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

| Hypothesis | Tested by |
|---|---|
| **H1** | M1 — Linear Regression |
| **H2** | M2 — Mixed Effects |
| **H3** | All 3 models compared |

:::

::: {.column width="40%"}

![](hypoth.jpeg){width="80%"}

:::

## 🌱 The Bean Profile {.smaller}
*Seven predictors — no yum yum taste scores allowed*

🌍 **Where it grew** — Altitude, Country*

🌱 **What it is** — Variety (Bourbon, Catuai, Caturra, Gesha, Typica, Other)

🔄 **How it was processed** — Washed, Natural, Honey

🔬 **Physical bean characteristics** — Color, Moisture, Defects (Cat 1 & 2)

*Country in Models 2 & 3 only*

## 📊 How Do These Beans Stack Up? {.smaller}

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
ggplot(coffee_clean, aes(x = `Total Cup Points`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "tan", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Total Cup Points", y = "Number of coffees") +
  theme_minimal()
```

📊 **plot type:** histogram

📍 **what we're looking at:** each bar shows how many coffees got that score.

🚨 **Range: ~80 to 87** — only 7 points fr. **restricted range alert** — limits how high our R² can go.

## 🏔️ Reaching New Heights {.smaller}

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
ggplot(coffee_clean, aes(x = Altitude_m, y = `Total Cup Points`)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "saddlebrown") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "darkred") +

```

📈 **Direction's right** (line slopes up → higher altitude = slightly higher score) **but lots of scatter** → altitude alone is a weak predictor

## 🗺️ Beans Around the World {.smaller}

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
top_countries <- coffee_clean %>% 
  count(`Country of Origin`) %>% filter(n >= 5) %>% pull(`Country of Origin`)

coffee_clean %>%
  filter(`Country of Origin` %in% top_countries) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(`Country of Origin`, `Total Cup Points`, median),
             y = `Total Cup Points`)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Total Cup Points") +
  theme_minimal()
```

📊 **plot type:** boxplot (one box per country)

📍 **what we're looking at:** each light blue box = ONE country. line in the middle = median (typical) score. ranked best at top → worst at bottom.

🇪🇹 Ethiopia tops — 🇧🇷 Brazil at the bottom → **country MATTERS**

## 📐 Drawing the Line in the Beans {.smaller}
*Model 1 — Multiple Linear Regression*

```r
m1 <- lm(`Total Cup Points` ~ Altitude_m + Variety_clean + 
                              Processing_clean + Color_clean +
                              `Moisture Percentage` + 
                              `Category One Defects` + 
                              `Category Two Defects`,
         data = coffee_clean)
```

📊 **R² = 0.35** — predictors explain 35% of variance (solid for restricted range fr)

🌟 **all of these passed the vibe check (p < 0.05):**

| Predictor | Effect | p-value |
|---|---|---|
| **Altitude** | +0.001 per meter | < 0.001 `***` ☑️ |
| **Variety: Gesha** | +1.42 vs Bourbon | < 0.001 `***` ☑️ |
| **Color: brownish** | +1.32 | 0.016 `*` ☑️ |
| **Cat 2 Defects** | −0.14 each | < 0.001 `***` ☑️ |

🎯 **H1 supported** ✅

## 🌐 Country Roads, Bean Me Home {.smaller}
*Model 2 — Mixed Effects (country as random effect)*

```r
m2 <- lmer(`Total Cup Points` ~ Altitude_m + Variety_clean + 
                                Processing_clean + Color_clean +
                                `Moisture Percentage` + 
                                `Category One Defects` + 
                                `Category Two Defects` +
                                (1 | `Country of Origin`),
           data = coffee_clean)
```

🏆 **ICC = 0.28** → 28% of unexplained variance lives at the country level fr

🌀 **plot twist:** Gesha LOST its significance 😪

> Gesha grows in already-good countries (Taiwan, Panama). once we let country take the credit, Gesha alone isn't special anymore.

🎯 **H2 supported** ✅

## 🌲 Can't See the Bean for the Trees {.smaller}
*Model 3 — Random Forest (500 trees averaged)*

```r
rf_model <- randomForest(TCP ~ ., 
                         data = train_rf, 
                         ntree = 500, 
                         importance = TRUE)
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5}
varImpPlot(rf_model, main = "Variable Importance")
```

📊 **plot type:** variable importance plot (two dot plots side-by-side)

📍 **what we're looking at:** RF tells us which predictors mattered most. dots farther right = more important.

🏆 **Top 3 predictors: Variety, Country, Altitude** — same story as M1 & M2

## 🏆 The Grind Final {.smaller}
*Test RMSE — lower is better*

📊 **plot type:** ranking table (test RMSE = how off our predictions are on average)

| Place | Model | Test RMSE |
|---|---|---|
| 🥇 | **M2: Mixed Effects** | **1.07** ← winner fr |
| 🥈 | M3: Random Forest | 1.19 |
| 🥉 | M1: Linear Regression | 1.30 |

. . .

❌ **H3 NOT supported** — RF came in 2nd, not 1st 😱

. . .

🤔 **Why tho?** small training set + restricted range + country effect is HIGHLY structured → the simpler structured model wins

## ☕ The Roast of My Findings {.smaller}

✅ **H1 supported** — altitude, variety, and defects all matter (Model 1 said so, all p < 0.05)

✅ **H2 supported** — country adds ~28% (ICC) of unexplained variance fr

❌ **H3 NOT supported** — random forest didn't beat the simpler models 🫠

. . .

🚧 **Limitations** (gotta be honest tho):

- 📉 Restricted TCP range (only 80–87) → caps how high R² can go
- 🇹🇼 Taiwan over-represented (61/207 samples)
- 🤏 Small dataset (n = 192)
- 🌱 83 rows lumped into variety "Other" (can't say much about minor varieties)

## 🎤 That's the Whole Latte It {.smaller}

> *"Sometimes the simpler model wins."*

. . .

🤔 **why I thought Random Forest would win:**
fancier ML model = usually better predictions, right?

. . .

🫠 **why I was wrong:**

- 🤏 small training set (only 155 rows) → RF couldn't flex
- 📉 restricted score range (only 80–87) → no big patterns to find
- 🌍 country effect was HIGHLY structured → mixed effects was literally built for this

. . .

✨ **Methodology > flexibility** — picking the right tool for the data structure beats picking the fanciest tool

. . .

## 🎁 Bonus: Why These 3 Models? {.smaller}
*In case you ask...*

🟢 **Why Linear Regression (M1)?**

Most interpretable — gives clean coefficients. You almost always start here in regression analysis to get a reference point.

. . .

🟡 **Why Mixed Effects (M2)?**

Country has 22 levels with super uneven sizes (Taiwan: 61, Madagascar: 1). Using country as a regular fixed effect would burn 21 degrees of freedom. Mixed effects handles clustered data efficiently.

. . .

🔴 **Why Random Forest (M3)?**

Captures non-linear patterns and interactions that linear models miss. Tests the explain ↔ predict tradeoff

. . .

🚫 **Why NOT others?**

- **Logistic regression** — only works for binary outcomes. TCP is continuous.
- **Just a decision tree** — Random Forest is basically a more robust version.
- **Polynomial regression** — EDA didn't show strong non-linear curves to justify it.
- **Fancy ML** (XGBoost, neural nets) — beyond what we covered in class + would overfit a 192-row dataset.
